sourceDocumentTitle: FLAREX Structured Research Database & Flame-in-Freefall Dossier

records.name: BASS / BASS-II (Burning and Suppression of Solids)
records.platform: International Space Station (Microgravity Science Glovebox) & Space Shuttle
records.dataAvailabilityLabel: Released in NASA PSI (ID 13000263), NTRS 20160000593 & NASA TM (2021)
records.overview: Investigated solid-material flame behavior, growth, and extinction in microgravity aboard Space Shuttle and ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox (BASS-II, 2014–2016) under varying airflow and sample conditions.
records.scientificPurpose: Measure microgravity solid-material flame behavior, flame spread rates, soot generation, and extinction boundaries under varied airflow, oxygen concentration, fuel thickness, and preheating.
records.background: Understanding how small solid fires behave and extinguish in ventilated microgravity cabins is foundational for ISS and exploration spacecraft fire protocols.
fuels: H2 / Mg / cotton (cited in NASA TM summary)
records.materialsAndGeometry: Thin and thick flat samples, acrylic slabs, spheres, and cylinders tested in opposed and concurrent microgravity flow.
environmentalVariables: Airflow speed (0–5 cm/s sensitivity; dim blue flames < 1 cm/s)
records.hardware: ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) with modular fan-driven flow duct; archived under PSI ID 13000263.
records.measurementMethods: Flame imagery/videos paired with extinction behavior observations, O2/CO2 gas concentration traces, and heat release rate analysis.
records.reportedFindings: Flames were sensitive to airflow speed in the 0–5 cm/s range in reported tests; some flames persisted below 1 cm/s as dim blue stable flames whose behavior changed with sudden airflow increases. A 2021 NASA report also noted extended flammability, higher soot, and limit heat release rates under 100 W.
records.scientificRelevance: Demonstrates that low-velocity cabin ventilation (< 5 cm/s) can sustain dim blue solid-fuel flames and alter extinction margins, directly informing spacecraft ventilation and suppression protocols.
limitations: Supplied NTRS record (20160000593) is a presentation/abstract, not a raw numerical dataset; do not fabricate time series or chart values.
Microgravity only: does not provide direct Lunar or Martian partial-gravity data.
Raw video/CSV sensor traces reside in NASA PSI (ID 13000263) and are not bundled locally.

quantitativeData.conditionContext: Airflow speed sensitivity range documented in BASS-II presentation/abstract (NTRS 20160000593); sudden airflow increases altered dim blue flames persisting below 1 cm/s.
quantitativeData.qualityNote: Presentation summary range; raw velocity/time-series traces reside in NASA PSI ID 13000263.

records.name: SAFFIRE (Spacecraft Fire Experiments I–III & Overview)
historicalNotes: Saffire-I launched aboard Cygnus OA-6 on 2016-03-22, berthed with ISS on 2016-03-25, and was initiated after unberthing via ground command with telemetry downlink before re-entry.
Supplied 2016 paper described Saffire-IV/V/VI as planned follow-on work; those historical plans must not be presented as proof of completion without independent verification.
records.overview: Large-scale microgravity material flammability experiments aboard uncrewed Cygnus cargo vehicles after ISS departure using ground-commanded initiation and pre-reentry telemetry downlink.
records.scientificPurpose: Demonstrate realistic spacecraft-scale fire length behavior, study whether flame growth reaches a steady size, and evaluate enclosure influence on flame spread and oxygen flammability limits.
records.background: ISS combustion racks restrict flame size for crew safety; uncrewed Cygnus vehicles allowed NASA Glenn researchers to test larger materials separated from crewed vehicles.
fuels: Saffire-I/III: 75% cotton / 25% fiberglass composite fabric (~0.4 m × 0.94 m, ~0.21 O2)
Saffire-II: 9 samples (~5 cm × 29 cm) of PMMA, silicone, composite fabric, and Nomex
records.materialsAndGeometry: Large composite fabric (~0.4 m × 0.94 m) for Saffire-I/III and nine 5 cm × 29 cm multi-material samples for Saffire-II inside spacious Cygnus enclosure.
environmentalVariables: Nominal cabin oxygen near 0.21 mole fraction (Saffire-I/III)
sensors: Inlet, flame-plume, and outlet temperature sensors
Two video cameras & green LED pyrolysis-length measurement
Four radiometers & thermocouples for flame stand-off distance
records.hardware: Uncrewed Cygnus large-scale fire test bay with ground-commanded ignition and telemetry downlink.
records.measurementMethods: Camera imagery as primary propagation/self-extinction diagnostic paired with O2/CO2, anemometer, radiometer, thermocouple, and pyrolysis-length telemetry.
records.reportedFindings: Enclosure size around a sample had more influence on flame spread than anticipated in the supplied summary; camera imagery served as primary diagnostic for Saffire-II propagation or self-extinction. Source paper also catalogs 7 technology gaps (low/partial-gravity flammability, detection, suppression, emergency crew mask, post-fire monitoring, cleanup, fire modeling).
records.scientificRelevance: Bridges small-sample rack tests to realistic spacecraft cabin volumes for vehicle-scale fire safety modeling.
limitations: Supplied sources are presentation/paper excerpts rather than full raw numerical datasets; historical Saffire-IV/V/VI plans must remain labeled as plans.
Results cannot directly simulate partial gravity (Lunar/Martian); they validate microgravity volumes only.
Dataset availability is split across PSI (13000367/68) and NTRS publications.

records.name: SAME / SAME-R (Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment)
records.dataAvailabilityLabel: PSI ID 13000294 (archived; conditional public release note)
records.principalInvestigator: Dr. David Urban (NASA Glenn Research Center) · Co-I: Dr. Zeng-Guang Yuan (NCMR) · Project Scientist: Dr. Gary Ruff (NASA GRC) · Partners: NIST, ZIN Technologies
records.sourceLabel: SAME / SAME-R Presentation Slides, NASA Overview & Technical Reports
records.overview: Measured low-gravity smoke-particle size and morphology (SAME & SAME-R reflight) to define spacecraft smoke-detector requirements and reduce false alarms.
records.scientificPurpose: Quantitatively determine low-gravity smoke particulate size (SAME) and obtain particle morphology while reducing size-distribution uncertainty against Shuttle experiments (SAME-R).
records.background: Following DAFT feasibility verification, SAME operated autonomously via ground-uplinked parameters with periodic crew consumable changes.
records.materialsAndGeometry: Refurbished/new sample carousels and thermal precipitators.
records.hardware: SAME / SAME-R hardware with sample carousels, thermal precipitators, and diagnostics unit.
records.measurementMethods: Autonomous ground-commanded particle size distribution and morphology sampling compared against smoke detector response curves.
records.reportedFindings: ISS particulates were larger on average than in Shuttle flights (likely due to cabin filters). NASA reports also note smoke yields 5–8x higher soot in microgravity contexts, informing dust-vs-smoke discrimination algorithms.
records.scientificRelevance: Essential for next-generation spacecraft smoke detectors (Artemis/Mars transit) to avoid false alarms from cabin dust while detecting true microgravity smoke.
limitations: Supplied SAME/SAME-R slides do not provide numerical particle sizes or morphology values; milestone dates in slides are historical plans, not current schedules.
PSI particle count logs (ID 13000294) are listed as likely archived / conditional ('if released').
Dossier notes 5–8x higher soot spread as a study-specific range rather than a universal multiplier.

quantitativeData.label: Reported Microgravity Smoke Soot Yield Factor
quantitativeData.conditionContext: Cited in dossier validation notes (p. 6) referencing NASA SAME findings on sparse/inconsistent smoke yield spread.
quantitativeData.sourceCitation: NASA SAME Experiment Overview (Dossier p. 1, p. 3, p. 6)
quantitativeData.qualityNote: Published relative range factor; raw P-Trak vs. smoke detector CSV logs require PSI ID 13000294 access.

records.name: FLEX & CFI-G (Fuel Ignition & COOL Diffusion Flames)

secondaryUrls.label: Search FLEX / Cool Flames on NASA NTRS

records.sourceLabel: NASA PSI & Univ. of Maryland / Phys.org Science Report
records.overview: Liquid-droplet combustion (FLEX) and porous-burner (CFI-G) microgravity experiments studying near-limit diffusion flames, inert-gas suppression, and sustained low-temperature cool diffusion flames.
records.scientificPurpose: Study near-limit diffusion flames, liquid-fuel droplet extinction, inert-gas suppressant effectiveness (CO2, He), chemical kinetics, and cool-flame combustion-model validation.
records.background: FLEX unexpectedly revealed long-lived cool diffusion flames after hot flame extinction; CFI-G (2021) created sustained steady cool diffusion flames on porous burners aboard the ISS using up to 85% O2/N2 mixtures.
fuels: Rich premixed gaseous fuels on porous burners (CFI-G)
records.materialsAndGeometry: Isolated 2–5 mm liquid droplets (FLEX in MDCA/CIR) and porous spherical burner (CFI-G).
environmentalVariables: Oxygen mole fraction: 0.10–0.50 (FLEX) & up to 85% O2/N2 spherical burner flow (CFI-G)
Diluents (N2, He) & Suppressants (CO2, He up to ~0.70 limit)
sensors: High-speed flame video cameras & radiation diagnostics
records.hardware: ISS Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) & CFI-G porous burner.
records.measurementMethods: Droplet burning rate, extinction diameters, radiation, soot temperature/concentration, chemiluminescence, and CO / formaldehyde (CH2O) species diagnostics.
records.reportedFindings: Discovered long-lived cool diffusion flames at ~600–1000 K; CFI-G created ~150 steady diffusion flames with distinct CO and CH2O chemistry. Documented FLEX ranges (0.10–0.50 O2, 0.5–1.0 atm, 2–5 mm droplets, CO2/He up to ~0.70) represent experimental variables rather than universal safety limits.
records.scientificRelevance: Reveals fundamental low-temperature combustion regimes invisible in terrestrial gravity, informing chemical kinetics models and spacecraft smoldering/suppression boundaries.
limitations: Experimental parameter ranges (0.10–0.50 O2, 0.5–1.0 atm, CO2/He suppressant concentration up to ~0.70) are experimental variables, NOT universal fire-suppression instructions or safety thresholds.
Microgravity behavior does NOT equal partial-gravity (Moon/Mars) data; CFI-G 85% O2/N2 flow is a specific inside-out burner configuration, not a general spacecraft atmosphere.
Specific FLEX-2/C PSI IDs are noted approximately (~130003xx) in the dossier; exact files require PSI access.

records.name: FLEX-2, FLEX-2J & FLEX-ICE-GA (Extended Droplet Combustion)
records.dataAvailabilityLabel: NASA Investigation Descriptions (NASA / JAXA / ASI Collaborations)
records.psiId: Listed under FLEX-2 / MDCA in NASA PSI

secondaryUrls.label: Search FLEX-2 / FLEX-2J on NASA NTRS

records.sourceLabel: NASA PSI Investigation Descriptions (FLEX-2, FLEX-2J, FLEX-ICE-GA)
records.overview: Extends FLEX droplet-combustion research to representative fuel mixtures, convective flow effects, 1D droplet arrays (NASA/JAXA FLEX-2J), and bio-derived surrogate fuels (ASI FLEX-ICE-GA).
records.scientificPurpose: Investigate multi-component fuel interactions, soot formation under convective flow, flame spread along droplet arrays, and green/bio-derived fuel surrogates in microgravity.
records.background: Follow-on campaigns utilizing the Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) inside ISS CIR with international partners JAXA and the Italian Space Agency (ASI).
records.materialsAndGeometry: Binary droplet arrays (FLEX-2) and 1D arrays of three fixed droplets plus movable droplets (FLEX-2J).
sensors: Chamber pressure and gas composition sensors
records.hardware: Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) in ISS Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR).
records.measurementMethods: Tracking droplet motion, burning time, flame spread rates along 1D droplet arrays, spacing, pressure, and gas composition.
records.reportedFindings: Supplied database records document configurations and partner test scopes (pure/mixed droplets, 3 fixed + movable array geometry in FLEX-2J, 50:50 surrogate blends in FLEX-ICE-GA); raw numerical outcomes reside in external PSI archives.
records.scientificRelevance: Extends idealized single-droplet microgravity combustion toward practical spacecraft/propulsion fuel mixtures and multi-droplet flame spread.
limitations: Configuration descriptions and planned test group counts are not equivalent to measured results; do not create synthetic experiment outcomes.
Microgravity only (no partial-gravity data).
No raw numerical dataset embedded in the loaded JSON database.

records.name: ACME — BRE (Burning Rate Emulator)
records.dataAvailabilityLabel: Flame heat flux & surface temps vs. gas flow in PSI

secondaryUrls.label: Search ACME BRE on NASA NTRS

records.overview: Simulates solid-fuel burning in microgravity using a flat porous gas burner inside the ISS Combustion Integrated Rack.
records.scientificPurpose: Improve fundamental understanding of solid materials flammability (such as paper and plastic analogs) in low gravity by controlling gaseous fuel flow to emulate solid pyrolysis.
records.background: Part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) laminar diffusion-flame suite aiming to improve combustion models and spacecraft fire prevention.
fuels: Gaseous fuel analogs simulating paper and plastic solid fuels
records.materialsAndGeometry: Porous gas burner emulating solid fuel surface regression and heat feedback.
records.hardware: ISS Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) porous gas burner insert.
records.measurementMethods: Measurement of flame heat flux and burner surface temperatures versus controlled gas flow to identify ignition and extinction limits.
records.reportedFindings: Dossier confirms BRE data (flame heat flux and surface temperatures vs. gas flow) are in PSI to characterize ignition and extinction of paper/plastic analogs.
records.scientificRelevance: Bridges simplified gaseous diffusion flames and complex solid-fuel flammability screening in spacecraft atmospheres.
limitations: Emulates solid-fuel burning via a porous gas burner rather than testing actual solid pyrolysis kinetics directly.
Microgravity only (no partial-gravity data).
NASA sources conflict on whether the broader ACME suite has five or six experiments.

records.name: ACME — E-FIELD Flames (Electric-Field Effects)
records.dataAvailabilityLabel: Ion currents & flame images; ACME release ongoing after analysis
records.psiId: ACME suite (PSI release pending full analysis)

secondaryUrls.label: Search E-FIELD Flames on NASA NTRS

records.overview: Studies ion-induced electric winds on microgravity coflow laminar diffusion flames by applying high-voltage electric fields up to 10 kV.
records.scientificPurpose: Understand flame ion production and electric-field flame control for emissions reduction and fundamental combustion physics.
records.background: Removing buoyancy in microgravity isolates subtle electrostatic ion forces ('electric wind') that alter flame shape and soot behavior.
fuels: Coflow laminar gaseous diffusion flame fuels
records.materialsAndGeometry: Coflow laminar burner inside ISS CIR with high-voltage electrode assembly.
environmentalVariables: Applied electric field voltage (up to 10 kV)
records.hardware: ISS CIR high-voltage electric-field coflow burner assembly.
records.measurementMethods: Recording flame ion currents versus applied voltage alongside flame shift and soot morphology images.
records.reportedFindings: An applied electric field up to 10 kV alters flame shape and soot behavior via ion-induced electric winds; full ACME datasets appear in PSI after analysis.
records.scientificRelevance: Clarifies flame ion chemistry and active electrostatic flame control; NOT a simulation of partial gravity.
limitations: CRITICAL: E-FIELD Flames tests electrostatic ion winds in microgravity — it must NOT be described as direct partial-gravity testing.
Not all ACME datasets are publicly released yet; images appear after post-flight analysis.
NASA sources conflict on whether the ACME suite contains five or six experiments.

quantitativeData.sourceCitation: NASA ACME E-FIELD Flames Description (Dossier p. 2 & p. 3)

records.name: ACME — CLD Flame, Flame Design & s-Flame (Suite Records)
records.dataAvailabilityLabel: No public PSI dataset yet (design papers & partner pubs only)

secondaryUrls.label: Search ACME CLD / s-Flame on NTRS

records.sourceLabel: NASA ACME Website & Partner Publications (Long et al., Proc. Combust. Inst. 2018)
records.overview: Additional experiments in the ACME modular CIR suite (CLD Flame, Flame Design, s-Flame, and CFI-G) studying soot inception/extinction, spherical flames, and oxygen-enriched combustion.
records.scientificPurpose: Investigate coflow soot volume fraction, oxygen-enriched spherical flames, flame extinction, and inside-out porous-burner cool flames across modular CIR hardware.
records.background: NASA source text in one paragraph mentions five experiments while the detailed list names six (BRE, CLD Flame, E-FIELD Flames, Flame Design, s-Flame, CFI-G); FLAREX preserves all six and flags the discrepancy.
fuels: Pure & highly diluted near-extinction laminar fuels (CLD Flame)
O2/N2 up to 85% oxygen porous-burner configuration (CFI-G)
records.materialsAndGeometry: Spherical, porous-burner, and coflow laminar diffusion burner geometries sharing modular ACME hardware in ISS CIR.
environmentalVariables: Oxygen / inert diluent ratios (including CFI-G up to 85% O2/N2 burner flow)
sensors: HD color camera, CH* and OH* imaging
Chamber pressure, SAMS-II acceleration, soot diagnostics
records.hardware: Modular ACME CIR insert with burners, igniter, gas-delivery system, and avionics.
records.measurementMethods: CH*/OH* chemiluminescence, color-ratio & thin-filament pyrometry, soot diagnostics, gas chromatography, and SAMS-II microgravity acceleration logging.
records.reportedFindings: In studied CLD Flame conditions, microgravity flames were taller, wider, cooler, and sootier than normal-gravity flames (one source reports 5–8× normal-gravity soot volume fraction; another context notes nearly 10× — kept study-specific). CFI-G performed high-oxygen microgravity tests (up to 85% O2/N2 from spherical burner). Remaining design datasets await full public PSI release.
records.scientificRelevance: Demonstrates active frontiers in laminar soot, spherical extinction, and oxygen-enriched combustion while preserving archive release caveats.
limitations: CRITICAL: Do not merge study-specific CLD Flame soot multipliers (5–8× vs. ~10×) into a single universal constant, and do not generalize CFI-G 85% O2/N2 burner flow as a spacecraft cabin atmosphere.
Planned / incomplete on-orbit data — do NOT treat planned datasets or design objectives as completed experimental results.
NASA sources disagree on whether the ACME suite has five or six experiments.

records.name: SLICE (Structure & Liftoff In Combustion Experiment)
records.overview: ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox investigation (2011–2012) of lifted laminar flames that bridged Shuttle-era SPICE and ACME's CLD Flame.
records.scientificPurpose: Capture flame-base stabilization and liftoff velocities versus fuel flow and burner size in microgravity to refine laminar combustion models.
records.background: Extended ground-based SPICE hardware into the ISS Glovebox as an early precursor to the ACME program.
records.materialsAndGeometry: Varied burner sizes generating lifted laminar jet flames.
records.hardware: ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox extending SPICE coflow hardware.
records.measurementMethods: Measured liftoff velocity versus fuel flow and burner size alongside flame structure imagery.
records.reportedFindings: Results (liftoff velocities vs. fuel and burner size) refined laminar flame stabilization models; flame images and velocity data were archived under PSI ID ACME-SLICE.
records.scientificRelevance: Provides continuity between Shuttle soot-onset studies (SPICE) and modern ISS CIR laminar flame experiments (ACME).
limitations: Historical ISS dataset (2011–2012).
Microgravity only; no partial-gravity data.
Raw image/velocity files reside in PSI (ACME-SLICE), not embedded in the dossier.

records.name: SPICE (Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment)
records.overview: Shuttle-era (1997) investigation mapping soot-onset smoke points in laminar coflow diffusion flames across multiple hydrocarbon fuels.
records.scientificPurpose: Determine exact conditions where laminar jet flames begin to emit soot in microgravity as a baseline for soot and combustion models.
records.background: Buoyancy strongly alters soot residence time on Earth; SPICE established a clean microgravity baseline across 250 tests.
records.hardware: Space Shuttle coflow combustion hardware (later extended for SLICE).
records.measurementMethods: Optical measurement of smoke-point distances, flame shapes, and smoke intensities across varied fuel flows.
records.reportedFindings: 250 microgravity tests produced over 70 smoke points across C3H6, C3H8, and C2H4 flames; flame shapes and smoke intensities are archived in PSI.
records.scientificRelevance: Core historical benchmark for microgravity soot inception and laminar flame radiation/smoke models.
limitations: Historical Shuttle-era dataset (>25 years old, 1997).
Dossier notes older datasets may lack complete metadata or require format normalization before ML ingestion.
Microgravity only (no partial-gravity data).

records.name: DAFT (Dust & Aerosol Feasibility Test)
records.platform: ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) & Cabin Modules
records.dataAvailabilityLabel: Instrument readings presumably in NASA archives (no PSI ID listed)
records.overview: ISS Glovebox and cabin aerosol feasibility experiment (2004–2005) verifying a portable ultrafine particle counter (P-Trak) in microgravity.
records.scientificPurpose: Verify ultrafine particle counting capability in microgravity ISS air using tracer aerosols, clearing the path for the full SAME smoke-sizing investigation.
records.background: Before calibrating smoke detectors in SAME, NASA needed to confirm portable aerosol instrumentation functioned accurately without gravity-driven settling.
environmentalVariables: ISS cabin module background particulate environment
sensors: P-Trak portable ultrafine particle counter (0.1–1 μm)
records.hardware: Portable P-Trak counter tested in ISS Glovebox and across ISS modules.
records.measurementMethods: P-Trak particle counts versus time in ISS cabin modules with and without released tracer aerosols.
records.reportedFindings: Verified P-Trak could count 0.1–1 μm particles in ISS air and confirmed low particulate levels in ISS with particles larger on average than on Earth, clearing the way for SAME.
records.scientificRelevance: Demonstrates hardware validation methodology for ultrafine spacecraft aerosol monitoring and dust-vs-smoke differentiation.
limitations: Feasibility / instrument verification test, not a direct combustion or flame-spread study.
No explicit PSI dataset ID listed in the dossier ('presumably in NASA archives').
Historical campaign (2004–2005).

quantitativeData.label: P-Trak Ultrafine Particle Detection Size Range
quantitativeData.conditionContext: Instrument operating size detection specification verified with tracer aerosols in ISS air.
quantitativeData.qualityNote: Instrument measurement range specification, not a combustion yield measurement.

records.name: Confined Combustion (Flames in Enclosures)
records.dataAvailabilityLabel: NASA Investigation ID 7886 · PSI ID 13000365 (conditional video release)
historicalNotes: NASA overview notes the first burn was performed aboard the ISS by astronaut Christina Koch on Christmas Eve 2019.
records.sourceLabel: NASA Investigation 7886 Overview & Case Western (Ya-Ting Liao)
records.overview: ISS investigation (ID 7886, 2019–2020) studying flame spread through differently shaped confined spaces and the influence of wall radiation and geometry in microgravity.
records.scientificPurpose: Isolate radiative and tunnel/wall-interaction fire-spread effects in microgravity where buoyant flow is eliminated, supporting building and vehicle fire-safety codes.
records.background: Real spacecraft compartments and terrestrial buildings involve walls and baffles that re-radiate heat and restrict flow; microgravity isolates these radiative enclosure effects.
records.materialsAndGeometry: Sibal fabric samples tested inside differently shaped confined enclosures with and without reflective surrounding walls.
records.measurementMethods: Measurement of flame spread rates, temperatures, and video of Sibal fabric flames with and without reflective baffles.
records.reportedFindings: Eliminating buoyant flow in microgravity successfully isolated radiative and tunnel wall effects, yielding flame spread and temperature context relevant to ISS modules, vehicles, and building fire codes.
records.scientificRelevance: Directly informs compartment-scale fire spread models for crewed habitats and terrestrial buildings/vehicles.
limitations: Supplied source is a NASA overview, not a full paper or raw numerical dataset; no numerical spread rates are available in the database.
SoFIE-OFFS is a separate investigation and must not be merged with Confined Combustion.
PSI flame videos (ID 13000365) are annotated as conditional ('if released'); microgravity only.

records.name: SoFIE-OFFS (Oscillatory Flow on Flame Spread)
records.dataAvailabilityLabel: No public PSI dataset yet (~30 experiments in NASA entry)

records.overview: Studies transient flame motion and flame spread through fine fuels under controlled non-steady (oscillatory) concurrent airflow in microgravity (2024-04 to 2026-07).
records.scientificPurpose: Isolate how transient oscillatory forced flow alters convective heating and ignition of fine fuels without buoyancy, informing both wildfire behavior research and spacecraft fire safety.
records.background: Distinct from Confined Combustion and SoFIE-MIST; developed by WPI, ZIN Technologies, and NASA Glenn Research Center for the SoFIE CIR insert.
fuels: Fine solid fuel samples under non-steady concurrent airflow
records.materialsAndGeometry: Fine solid fuels configured in SoFIE oscillatory forced-flow test section.
records.hardware: ISS Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) SoFIE insert (WPI / ZIN Technologies / NASA GRC).
records.measurementMethods: Controlled non-steady forced airflow applied to observe transient flame motion, convective heating, and fine-fuel ignition.
records.reportedFindings: NASA entry describes approximately 30 experiments examining transient convective heating under oscillatory flow; no numerical results or public PSI datasets are included yet.
records.scientificRelevance: Bridges spacecraft non-steady cabin ventilation hazards and terrestrial wildfire convective-ignition physics.
limitations: CRITICAL: Listed period (2024-04 to 2026-07) and ~30 experiment count are source metadata, NOT proof that all tests are completed or publicly available.
Separate investigation from Confined Combustion and SoFIE-MIST.

records.sourceLabel: Underwriters Laboratories Presentation at 2020 NASA Aerospace Battery Workshop
records.overview: Terrestrial (1g) Underwriters Laboratories presentation characterizing fire hazards, thermal runaway, vent gases, and smoke for selected LFP cylindrical and NMC prismatic Li-ion configurations at 100% SOC using UL 9540A heating.
records.scientificPurpose: Characterize thermal runaway propagation, peak temperatures, and vent gas volumes/compositions (CO, H2, HF) across selected LFP and NMC cell, module, and battery configurations.
records.background: High-energy Li-ion cells are critical for spacecraft and surface systems, but NASA has no in-flight microgravity battery fire dataset; this UL workshop presentation provides terrestrial hazard context only.
records.materialsAndGeometry: Selected LFP cylindrical and NMC prismatic cells, modules, and battery packs heated under UL 9540A profile.
environmentalVariables: 1g Earth laboratory atmosphere (NOT microgravity or ISS data)
100% state of charge (SOC) · UL 9540A heating profile
sensors: Thermal runaway temperature probes (1459°C NMC / 661°C LFP test examples)
Vent gas composition & volume analyzers (CO, H2, HF)
records.hardware: Ground-based UL 9540A thermal runaway test apparatus.
records.measurementMethods: UL 9540A thermal heating of cells/modules/batteries tracking maximum temperatures, propagation behavior, and single-cell gas volumes/compositions.
records.reportedFindings: In the reported 1g tests, NMC modules/battery propagated with external fire (example max 1459°C), whereas LFP modules/battery showed thermal-runaway propagation without external flaming (example max 661°C). Single-cell gas sample differences also reflect differing cell capacities/configurations, so direct chemistry-only generalizations are invalid.
records.scientificRelevance: Highlights why thermal runaway and visible fire are not synonymous, why single-cell tests cannot alone predict pack behavior, and why in-flight microgravity battery fire data remain an urgent gap.
limitations: CRITICAL: Ground-based terrestrial 1g tests performed by UL ONLY — NOT microgravity or ISS data, and NOT performed by NASA.
Example max temperatures (1459°C NMC, 661°C LFP) are test-specific for selected cell capacities/configurations, NOT universal chemistry properties.
Do NOT mix into microgravity dataset charts or microgravity ML training sets.

records.name: Solid Fuel Combustion in Partial & Micro-Gravity (Scientific Review & PSI Audit)
records.platform: Cross-Archive Literature Synthesis (PSI, NTRS, ISS & Shuttle)
records.dataAvailabilityLabel: Review paper & structured database covering 15+ NASA/partner records
records.sourceLabel: Solid Fuel Combustion in Partial and Micro-Gravity Review & FLAREX Database
records.overview: Synthesizes solid-fuel combustion physics (cellulosics, plastics, composites, battery electrodes) and fire-safety knowledge gaps in microgravity and partial gravity alongside NASA PSI dataset audits.
records.scientificPurpose: Review coupled solid/gas physics (reduced buoyancy, radiation, smoldering, pyrolysis) and establish research gaps across DNS/LES, solid-phase kinetics, and partial-gravity validation.
records.background: Combines the scientific review 'Solid Fuel Combustion in Partial and Micro-Gravity' with FLAREX's pre-event PSI quality audit.
fuels: Cellulosic materials, plastics, hydrocarbons, composites, and battery electrode materials
records.materialsAndGeometry: Multi-scale solid fuels, charring/swelling polymers, pyrolysate transport, and coupled solid/gas configurations.
environmentalVariables: Imposed airflow, radiative feedback, pressure & material geometry
sensors: Synthesis of optical flame video, radiometry, P-Trak, O2/CO2, heat flux, and chemiluminescence diagnostics
records.hardware: Cross-platform synthesis (Shuttle, ISS MSG, ISS CIR, Cygnus, Ground Lab) and DNS/LES multiphysics models.
records.measurementMethods: Literature synthesis & 6-point PSI dataset quality audit covering DNS, LES, solid decomposition, charring/smoldering, and in-depth radiation modeling.
records.reportedFindings: Reduced gravity weakens buoyancy so diffusion, radiation, geometry, and imposed flow dominate. BASS/BASS-II and Saffire confirm material/geometry/flow sensitivity; partial-gravity concurrent-flow spread evidence remains limited and uncertain; 9 key research gaps (solid kinetics, pyrolysate transport, deformation/swelling, scale, partial-gravity validation, battery runaway, advanced diagnostics, coupled models) are identified.
records.scientificRelevance: Establishes the scientific gap taxonomy, modeling priorities, and strict provenance rules implemented across FLAREX.
limitations: Literature review ONLY — not a single experiment dataset; avoid turning its discussion into operational fire-management advice.
Summarizes secondary NASA pages, TMs, press releases, and workshop decks without embedding raw AVI/CSV files.
